definition: The MM algorithm is an iterative optimization method which exploits the convexity of a function in order to find its maxima or minima.
details: The MM stands for “Majorize-Minimization” or “Minorize-Maximization”, depending on whether the desired optimization is a minimization or a maximization. Despite the name, MM itself is not an algorithm, but a family of optimization algorithms that follow the same construction pattern. The expectation–maximization algorithm can be treated as a special case of the MM algorithm. However, in the EM algorithm conditional expectations are usually involved, while in the MM algorithm convexity and inequalities are the main focus, and it is easier to understand and apply in most cases.

explainer.lead: The MM algorithm is an iterative optimization method that exploits the convexity of a function to find its maxima or minima. It matters because it is a family of algorithms built on one construction pattern, with EM as a special case.

tiers.eli5: Instead of leaping straight to the best answer, you repeatedly take a safe step by working with a simpler version of the problem.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply the Majorize-Minimization form for minimization or Minorize-Maximization for maximization, choosing the right one for the goal. A pitfall is confusion with EM: EM is a special case, but EM usually involves conditional expectations while MM relies on convexity and inequalities.
tiers.paperLevel: An iterative optimization family: Majorize-Minimization when minimizing and Minorize-Maximization when maximizing. MM is not a single algorithm but a family following the same construction pattern; the expectation–maximization algorithm is a special case, though EM usually involves conditional expectations while MM involves convexity and inequalities.

explainer.example: A statistician minimizing a difficult objective repeatedly optimizes a simpler majorizing function until the result converges.
